title: Get Wisdom, Guard Your Heart
summary: The father passes on what his own father taught him: get wisdom, love her, and she will protect and honor you. He then contrasts the path of the righteous, which grows brighter like the dawn, with the dark way of the wicked, who cannot sleep until they have done harm. Finally he urges his son to guard his heart, his speech, his eyes, and his steps, and not to swerve from the straight path.
story: Chapters 1 to 3 introduced wisdom, described how to find her, and showed her fruits. Chapter 4 deepens the picture in two ways. It shows that wisdom is handed down across generations, from grandfather to father to son. And it presses the book's central image of two ways further than before, with one path growing brighter and the other darker. The chapter also sets up the next three chapters, which return in detail to the danger of the forbidden woman, by insisting that the heart is where every path begins.
historical:
The chapter gives no historical markers, and its setting is the timeless one of a household. Verses 3 and 4 are unusual: the father speaks of being a tender child, the only son of his mother, and quotes his own father's teaching. Because the book is linked with Solomon, some readers have heard this as Solomon remembering David and Bathsheba, and 1 Chronicles 22 and 28 and 1 Kings 2 do record David's charges to Solomon. The chapter itself doesn't name them, however, and the phrase only child probably means beloved or unique rather than making a claim about David's family, since Bathsheba had other sons (1 Chronicles 3:5). It may simply be the voice of every teaching father, remembering how he was taught.

The practice it describes was real across the ancient Near East: instruction was passed down orally in families and among scribes, and the authority of a teaching rested partly on its age and its line of transmission.
cultural:
In the ancient world the heart was not mainly the seat of emotion, as it is in English. In Hebrew thought, the heart (lev) was the center of the inner person: the place of thinking, deciding, remembering, and desiring, what we might call the mind and will together. Guarding the heart (verse 23) therefore means guarding one's whole inner orientation, the source from which choices, words, and actions flow. The image of springs flowing from it would be vivid in a dry land where a reliable spring determined where a town could exist.

Paths and roads were also concrete. Travel was on foot on uneven tracks, where stones, ruts, and hidden holes could trip a traveler, and darkness made travel truly dangerous. A level path (verse 26) was one cleared and smoothed. The wicked who eat the bread of wickedness and drink the wine of violence (verse 17) live on what they take from others, as a person lives on daily food and drink.
literary: The chapter contains three instruction speeches, each beginning with a call to listen (verses 1, 10, and 20). The first includes a speech within a speech, the grandfather's words quoted in verses 4 to 9, with its piling up of the command get wisdom and its images of embracing and honoring wisdom as a bride or patron who crowns the one who loves her. The second centers on the contrast between the two paths, drawn as dawn light growing to midday and deep darkness where people stumble without knowing why. The third moves through the body, heart, mouth, lips, eyes, and feet, as if the father were checking his son from the inside out.

outline.t: Wisdom handed down: my father taught me
Two paths: the dawn and the darkness
Guard your heart, mouth, eyes, and feet

doctrines.note: Wisdom is to be acquired at any cost, loved, and held onto. It is not a possession that comes automatically with age; it must be chosen and pursued, and it shapes the whole direction of life.

The chapter pictures three generations handing on wisdom, echoing Deuteronomy 6:7, where parents are told to teach God's words to their children. Faith and wisdom are meant to be passed down deliberately.
Verse 23 locates the source of human life and conduct in the heart. What a person is inwardly determines where he goes outwardly, so moral formation must reach the inner person, not only behavior.

words.note: Qanah, to acquire or buy. It is the ordinary word for purchasing goods or property, used four times here in commands to get wisdom and understanding. Verse 7 pushes it hard: whatever else you acquire, acquire understanding. Wisdom is worth spending everything on, the way a merchant would pay any price for a treasure.

Lev, heart. In Hebrew the heart is the inner self, the place of mind, will, memory, and desire. Verse 4 asks the heart to lay hold of words, and verse 23 names it as the source of the springs of life. Hebrew has little separation between thinking and feeling; the heart does both.

Natsar, to watch or guard. It describes a watchman keeping a city or a vineyard, or someone preserving something valuable. In verse 6 wisdom guards the one who loves her, and in verse 23 the son is told to guard his own heart. Wisdom protects those who protect it.

christ: Luke tells us that the boy Jesus grew in wisdom and stature and in favor with God and man (Luke 2:52), taking up the language of Proverbs to describe a son formed in a faithful home. Jesus later taught that what comes out of the heart is what defiles a person (Mark 7:20-23), a direct echo of verse 23's claim that life flows from the heart. The image of the path of the righteous as growing light is fulfilled, in the New Testament's reading, in Jesus as the light of the world, whose followers will not walk in darkness (John 8:12). These are thematic links: the chapter describes the wise son, and the Gospels present Jesus as the Son who fully embodied that wisdom.
questions: Who handed wisdom down to you, and what would you want to pass on to the next generation?
If the heart is the source of the springs of life, what are you allowing to shape your heart day by day?
Verse 19 says the wicked don't know what makes them stumble. How can a person become aware of what is tripping them up?
